claim: Acute depletion of TBP in mouse embryonic stem cells has no global effect on ongoing Pol II transcription.
source: Here, we report instead that acute depletion of TBP in mouse embryonic stem cells has no global effect on ongoing Pol II transcription.
evidence: Supported by Pol II CUT&Tag and NET-seq data showing no global changes in Pol II occupancy or nascent RNA levels upon TBP depletion (Figure 1C-F).

claim: Acute TBP depletion severely impairs RNA Polymerase III initiation.
source: In contrast, acute TBP depletion severely impairs RNA Polymerase III initiation.
evidence: Supported by Pol III CUT&Tag and NET-seq data showing major decreases in Pol III occupancy and activity at tRNA genes upon TBP depletion (Figure 2A-C).

claim: Pol II transcriptional induction occurs normally upon TBP depletion.
source: Furthermore, Pol II transcriptional induction occurs normally upon TBP depletion.
evidence: Supported by heat shock and retinoic acid differentiation experiments showing normal gene induction when TBP is depleted (Figure 3).

claim: TBP-independent transcription mechanism is not due to functional redundancy with the TBP paralog TRF2.
source: This TBP-independent transcription mechanism is not due to a functional redundancy with the TBP paralog TRF2, though TRF2 also binds to promoters of transcribed genes.
evidence: Supported by data showing that TRF2 knock-out combined with TBP depletion has no global effect on Pol II transcription (Figure 4E-F).

claim: TRF2 binds to promoters of transcribed genes in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: This TBP-independent transcription mechanism is not due to a functional redundancy with the TBP paralog TRF2, though TRF2 also binds to promoters of transcribed genes.
evidence: Supported by HA-TRF2 CUT&Tag data showing TRF2 binding at promoters of active genes (Figure 4C-D).

claim: The TFIID complex can form when TBP is depleted.
source: Rather, we show that the TFIID complex can form and, despite having reduced TAF4 and TFIIA binding when TBP is depleted, the Pol II machinery is sufficiently robust in sustaining TBP-independent transcription.
evidence: Supported by TAF4 IP-MS data showing similar levels of TAF subunits in control and TBP-depleted conditions (Figure 5C).

claim: TAF4 binding is reduced when TBP is depleted.
source: Rather, we show that the TFIID complex can form and, despite having reduced TAF4 and TFIIA binding when TBP is depleted, the Pol II machinery is sufficiently robust in sustaining TBP-independent transcription.
evidence: Supported by TAF4 CUT&Tag data showing approximately 65% decrease in TAF4 occupancy at promoters upon TBP depletion (Figure 6B-C).

claim: TFIIA binding is reduced when TBP is depleted.
source: Rather, we show that the TFIID complex can form and, despite having reduced TAF4 and TFIIA binding when TBP is depleted, the Pol II machinery is sufficiently robust in sustaining TBP-independent transcription.
evidence: Supported by TFIIA CUT&Tag data showing approximately 60% decrease in TFIIA occupancy at promoters upon TBP depletion (Figure 6B-C).

claim: The Pol II machinery is sufficiently robust in sustaining TBP-independent transcription.
source: Rather, we show that the TFIID complex can form and, despite having reduced TAF4 and TFIIA binding when TBP is depleted, the Pol II machinery is sufficiently robust in sustaining TBP-independent transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that despite reduced TAF4 and TFIIA binding, Pol II transcription remains unaffected upon TBP depletion.

claim: Transcription by RNA Polymerase II is initiated by the hierarchical assembly of the pre-initiation complex onto promoter DNA.
source: Transcription by RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) is initiated by the hierarchical assembly of the pre-initiation complex onto promoter DNA.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by decades of research cited in the introduction.

claim: Decades of research have shown that TBP is essential for Pol II loading and initiation.
source: Decades of research have shown that the TATA-box binding protein (TBP) is essential for Pol II loading and initiation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge based on previous research cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: The GTF TFIID is composed of TBP and 13-14 evolutionarily conserved TBP-associated factors (TAFs).
source: First, the GTF TFIID, composed of the TATA-box binding protein (TBP) and 13–14 evolutionarily conserved TBP-associated factors (TAFs), binds onto gene promoters (Reinberg et al., 1987; Buratowski et al., 1989; Dynlacht et al., 1991; Cormack and Struhl, 1992; Tanese et al., 1991), which triggers the recruitment of TFIIA and TFIIB (Reinberg et al., 1987; Buratowski et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: TFIID binding onto gene promoters triggers the recruitment of TFIIA and TFIIB.
source: First, the GTF TFIID, composed of the TATA-box binding protein (TBP) and 13–14 evolutionarily conserved TBP-associated factors (TAFs), binds onto gene promoters (Reinberg et al., 1987; Buratowski et al., 1989; Dynlacht et al., 1991; Cormack and Struhl, 1992; Tanese et al., 1991), which triggers the recruitment of TFIIA and TFIIB (Reinberg et al., 1987; Buratowski et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pol II is loaded onto the promoter along with TFIIF.
source: Pol II is then loaded onto the promoter along with TFIIF (Reinberg et al., 1987; Buratowski et al., 1989; Buratowski et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The binding of TFIIE and TFIIH completes the pre-initiation complex.
source: The binding of TFIIE and TFIIH completes the PIC, upon which the enzymatic activity of TFIIH unwinds DNA to form a transcription bubble, allowing for Pol II elongation and the incorporation of nucleotides into the nascent RNA (Reinberg et al., 1987; Buratowski et al., 1989; Rimel and Taatjes, 2018).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The enzymatic activity of TFIIH unwinds DNA to form a transcription bubble.
source: The binding of TFIIE and TFIIH completes the PIC, upon which the enzymatic activity of TFIIH unwinds DNA to form a transcription bubble, allowing for Pol II elongation and the incorporation of nucleotides into the nascent RNA (Reinberg et al., 1987; Buratowski et al., 1989; Rimel and Taatjes, 2018).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TBP was first discovered to recognize and bind to the TATA-box (TATAAA consensus sequence) in gene promoters in vitro.
source: TBP was first discovered to recognize and bind to the TATA-box (TATAAA consensus sequence) in gene promoters in vitro (Nakajima et al., 1988; Hoey et al., 1990; Buratowski et al., 1988), though subsequent studies show that TBP binds to active gene promoters in vivo regardless of the presence of a TATA sequence (Kim and Iyer, 2004; Pugh and Venters, 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TBP binds to active gene promoters in vivo regardless of the presence of a TATA sequence.
source: TBP was first discovered to recognize and bind to the TATA-box (TATAAA consensus sequence) in gene promoters in vitro (Nakajima et al., 1988; Hoey et al., 1990; Buratowski et al., 1988), though subsequent studies show that TBP binds to active gene promoters in vivo regardless of the presence of a TATA sequence (Kim and Iyer, 2004; Pugh and Venters, 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of functional TBP led to decreased GTF and Pol II recruitment and transcription in vivo in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Early studies in Saccharomyces cerevisiae expressing TBP mutations show that the loss of functional TBP led to decreased GTF and Pol II recruitment and transcription in vivo (Klages and Strubin, 1995; Kim et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Acute TBP depletion in yeast cells via the anchor-away system led to a rapid, genome-wide loss of Pol II and GTF occupancy.
source: More recently, acute TBP depletion in yeast cells via the anchor-away system led to a rapid, genome-wide loss of Pol II and GTF occupancy (Petrenko et al., 2017; Petrenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TBP is involved in RNA Pol I and III transcription.
source: In addition to facilitating Pol II transcription, TBP is also involved in at least two other RNA polymerases found in eukaryotes, and conditional inactivation of TBP in yeast led to a global decrease in both RNA Pol I and III transcriptional activity (Cormack and Struhl, 1992; Kwon and Green, 1994; Schröder et al., 2003; Shen et al., 1998; White et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Conditional inactivation of TBP in yeast led to a global decrease in both RNA Pol I and III transcriptional activity.
source: In addition to facilitating Pol II transcription, TBP is also involved in at least two other RNA polymerases found in eukaryotes, and conditional inactivation of TBP in yeast led to a global decrease in both RNA Pol I and III transcriptional activity (Cormack and Struhl, 1992; Kwon and Green, 1994; Schröder et al., 2003; Shen et al., 1998; White et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In vitro experiments using purified proteins from yeast and human cells confirm the role of TBP in the three main RNA polymerases.
source: In vitro experiments using purified proteins from yeast and human cells also confirm the role of TBP in the three main RNA polymerases (Goodrich and Tjian, 1994; Burley and Roeder, 1996).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mouse embryos harboring a homozygous TBP knock-out, which were viable up to ~40 cell stage of embryogenesis, still displayed normal levels of Pol II transcription.
source: However, mouse embryos harboring a homozygous TBP knock-out, which were viable up to ~40 cell stage of embryogenesis, still displayed normal levels of Pol II transcription (Martianov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Acute depletion of TBP in mouse embryonic stem cells showed that global transcription levels remained unaffected.
source: Furthermore, acute depletion of TBP in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) showed that global transcription levels remained unaffected (Teves et al., 2018), raising the question of how Pol II transcription occurs in the absence of TBP in these cases.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TBP may be required only for the initial round of activation, but ongoing transcription may no longer need TBP.
source: One, TBP may be required only for the initial round of activation, but ongoing transcription may no longer needed for TBP.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain TBP-independent transcription.

claim: The impairment of the reactivation of genes following mitosis when TBP is depleted would support the mechanism that TBP is required only for initial activation.
source: The impairment of the reactivation of genes following mitosis when TBP is depleted (Teves et al., 2018) would support this mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Metazoan-specific TBP paralogs could functionally replace TBP.
source: Two, metazoan-specific TBP paralogs could functionally replace TBP.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain TBP-independent transcription.

claim: In some species, TBP paralogs have been found to bind onto genomic loci distinct from TBP and regulate cell type-specific genes.
source: In some species, TBP paralogs have been found to bind onto genomic loci distinct from TBP and regulate cell type-specific genes (Akhtar and Veenstra, 2009; Kedmi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TBP-related factors TRF1 and TRF2, first discovered in Drosophila, are able to substitute for TBP in TATA transcriptional systems.
source: Furthermore, TBP-related factors TRF1 and TRF2, first discovered in Drosophila, are also able to substitute for TBP in TATA transcriptional systems (Crowley et al., 1993; Hansen et al., 1997; Rabenstein et al., 1999; Holmes and Tjian, 2000).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TRF3, a third vertebrate-specific paralog, mediates transcription of oocyte-specific genes through a non-canonical complex with TFIIA/TFIIB.
source: A third vertebrate-specific paralog, TRF3, mediates transcription of oocyte-specific genes through a non-canonical complex with TFIIA/TFIIB (Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A TAF-containing complex could facilitate Pol II transcription without TBP.
source: Three, a TAF-containing complex could facilitate Pol II transcription without TBP.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain TBP-independent transcription.

claim: The TBP-free TAF-containing complex (TFTC) isolated from human cells can support in vitro Pol II transcription without TBP or TFIID.
source: Indeed, several TAF complexes have been identified, including the TBP-free TAF-containing complex (TFTC) isolated from human cells that can support in vitro Pol II transcription without TBP or TFIID (Wieczorek et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TFTC corresponds to the SAGA (Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase) complex, a conserved eukaryotic co-activator with histone acetyltransferase activity.
source: TFTC was subsequently shown to correspond to the SAGA (Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase) complex, a conserved eukaryotic co-activator with histone acetyltransferase activity (Cheon et al., 2020), which has been shown to act somewhat redundantly with TFIID in yeast (Donczew et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SAGA has been shown to act somewhat redundantly with TFIID in yeast.
source: TFTC was subsequently shown to correspond to the SAGA (Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase) complex, a conserved eukaryotic co-activator with histone acetyltransferase activity (Cheon et al., 2020), which has been shown to act somewhat redundantly with TFIID in yeast (Donczew et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA resulted in no major effects on cell viability.
source: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA (+IAA) resulted in no major effects on cell viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) with over ~90% depletion of mAID-TBP as detected by immunofluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), by western blot of whole cell lysates (Figure 1B) and of subcellular fractions, including chromatin-bound fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA resulted in over ~90% depletion of mAID-TBP as detected by immunofluorescence.
source: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA (+IAA) resulted in no major effects on cell viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) with over ~90% depletion of mAID-TBP as detected by immunofluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), by western blot of whole cell lysates (Figure 1B) and of subcellular fractions, including chromatin-bound fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA resulted in over ~90% depletion of mAID-TBP as detected by western blot of whole cell lysates.
source: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA (+IAA) resulted in no major effects on cell viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) with over ~90% depletion of mAID-TBP as detected by immunofluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), by western blot of whole cell lysates (Figure 1B) and of subcellular fractions, including chromatin-bound fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA resulted in over ~90% depletion of mAID-TBP in subcellular fractions, including chromatin-bound fractions.
source: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA (+IAA) resulted in no major effects on cell viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) with over ~90% depletion of mAID-TBP as detected by immunofluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), by western blot of whole cell lysates (Figure 1B) and of subcellular fractions, including chromatin-bound fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data of subcellular fractions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A large decrease in bound TBP at Gapdh and Hspa1a was detected by ChIP-qPCR after IAA treatment.
source: We also detected a large decrease in bound TBP at Gapdh and Hspa1a as measured by ChIP-qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: After 6 and 16 hr of IAA treatment, over ~80% decrease in TBP occupancy at promoters of genes was observed.
source: After 6 and 16 hr of IAA treatment, we observed a large depletion of bound TBP (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), and when quantified at the promoters of genes (herein defined as –250 bp to TSS) relative to control conditions, we observed over ~80% decrease (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TBP binds at high levels on the promoters and gene bodies of Gapdh and Actb in control samples.
source: We observed that in control samples, Pol II binds at high levels on the promoters and gene bodies of Gapdh and Actb (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by gene browser tracks shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: After 6 hr of IAA treatment, Pol II occupancy at the Gapdh and Actb loci remained largely unchanged.
source: After 6 hr of IAA treatment, Pol II occupancy at the Gapdh and Actb loci remained largely unchanged.
evidence: Supported by gene browser tracks shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Prolonged IAA treatment (16 hr) showed no global effects on Pol II occupancy.
source: Prolonged IAA treatment (16 hr) also showed no global effects on Pol II occupancy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by Pol II CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Pearson correlation analysis shows high correlation coefficients (0.85–0.97) across both control and IAA-treated samples regardless of treatment times for Pol II CUT&Tag.
source: Indeed, Pearson correlation analysis using 10 kb bins of all Pol II CUT&Tag replicates show high correlation coefficients (0.85–0.97) across both control and IAA-treated samples regardless of treatment times, showing no global differences in Pol II occupancy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Comparable intronic and exonic signals in Gapdh and Actb genes were detected by NET-seq for both control and IAA-treated samples.
source: After normalization with spike-in controls, we detected comparable intronic and exonic signals in Gapdh and Actb genes for both control and IAA-treated samples (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by NET-seq data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Genes with the largest decrease in TBP occupancy after IAA treatment showed no change in Pol II occupancy and nascent RNA levels.
source: Using k-means clustering, we identified genes with the largest decrease in TBP occupancy after IAA treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A). Despite these genes experiencing the largest depletion of TBP upon IAA treatment, Pol II occupancy and nascent RNA levels remained unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: No difference in Pol II occupancy and NET-seq signal was observed for promoters containing or lacking a defined TATA-box sequence upon TBP depletion.
source: We also observed no difference in Pol II occupancy and NET-seq signal for promoters containing or lacking a defined TATA-box sequence upon TBP depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Approximately 99.9% of genes do not display significant changes in Pol II occupancy or NET-seq signal upon TBP depletion.
source: Consistent with the global average plots and heatmaps, DGE analysis of both Pol II and NET-seq data in control vs. IAA-treated samples show that ~99.9% of genes do not display significant changes upon TBP depletion (black dots in Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 29 genes showed significant downregulation with approximately one- to fourfold decrease in Pol II occupancy upon IAA treatment.
source: However, 29 genes showed significant downregulation with approximately one- to fourfold decrease in Pol II occupancy upon IAA treatment (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by DGE analysis and listed in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Prolonged auxin treatment (16 hr) resulted in only two genes showing significant downregulation in Pol II occupancy.
source: However, prolonged auxin treatment (16 hr) was also analyzed using DGE analysis and only two genes showed a significant downregulation in Pol II occupancy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that some of the identified downregulated genes at 6 hr may be false positives.
evidence: Supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Only a select number of genes may be affected upon TBP depletion in mouse ESCs.
source: Therefore, in contrast to the global effects of TBP depletion in yeast cells, these findings show that only a select number of genes may be affected upon TBP depletion in mouse ESCs.
evidence: Inferred from the DGE analysis showing that only a small number of genes are significantly affected.

claim: Pol III transcribes all of the tRNAs, the 5S ribosomal RNA, 7SK, and 7SL RNAs, the U6 spliceosomal RNA, and other groups of non-coding RNAs.
source: Whereas Pol II transcribes protein coding genes, Pol III transcribes all of the tRNAs, the 5S ribosomal RNA, 7SK, and 7SL RNAs, the U6 spliceosomal RNA, and other groups of non-coding RNAs that are critical for cellular functions (Roeder and Rutter, 1970; Weinmann and Roeder, 1974; Price and Penman, 1972; Zieve et al., 1977; Reddy et al., 1987; Wolin and Steitz, 1983; Martignetti and Brosius, 1995).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA reduced global TBP protein levels, but protein levels of the RPC7 subunit of Pol III do not change.
source: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA reduced global TBP protein levels, but protein levels of the RPC7 subunit of Pol III do not change, as confirmed by western blot of C64 whole cell lysates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Pol III protein levels are unaffected by TBP depletion.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pol III protein levels are unaffected by TBP depletion.
source: Treatment of C64 cells with 6 hr of IAA reduced global TBP protein levels, but protein levels of the RPC7 subunit of Pol III do not change, as confirmed by western blot of C64 whole cell lysates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Pol III protein levels are unaffected by TBP depletion.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RPC7 protein levels do not change upon TBP depletion.

claim: Pol III binds at high levels on tRNA genes LeuCAA and GlnCTG in control samples.
source: Pol III binds at high levels on tRNA genes LeuCAA and GlnCTG in control samples, and upon TBP depletion, we observed a major decrease in Pol III occupancy at these tRNA genes and across each individual replicate (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Pol III CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Upon TBP depletion, a major decrease in Pol III occupancy at tRNA genes LeuCAA and GlnCTG was observed.
source: Pol III binds at high levels on tRNA genes LeuCAA and GlnCTG in control samples, and upon TBP depletion, we observed a major decrease in Pol III occupancy at these tRNA genes and across each individual replicate (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Pol III CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A global decrease in Pol III occupancy across all tRNAs was observed upon TBP depletion.
source: We then plotted the Pol III occupancy in a 2 kb window surrounding the TSS for all tRNAs in control and TBP-depleted cells and observed a global decrease in Pol III occupancy across all tRNAs upon TBP depletion (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Pol III CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: High signals for tRNA genes LeuCAA and GlnCTG were detected by NET-seq in control cells, with a two- to threefold decrease upon IAA treatment.
source: We detected high signals for tRNA genes LeuCAA and GlnCTG in control cells, and observed a two- to threefold decrease upon IAA treatment (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by NET-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TBP is required for the transcription of tRNAs by Pol III in mESCs.
source: Therefore, TBP is required for the transcription of tRNAs by Pol III in mESCs, consistent with previous studies in yeast and in vitro systems (Cormack and Struhl, 1992; White et al., 1992; Han et al., 2018; Wang and Stumph, 1995).
evidence: Supported by Pol III CUT&Tag and NET-seq data showing decreased Pol III activity at tRNA genes upon TBP depletion, consistent with previous studies.

claim: The consistent role of TBP in Pol III transcription contrasts strikingly with the TBP-independent Pol II transcription in mESCs.
source: Importantly, the consistent role of TBP in Pol III transcription contrasts strikingly with the TBP-independent Pol II transcription in mESCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the effects of TBP depletion on Pol II versus Pol III transcription.

claim: Depletion of TBP in mESCs specifically during mitosis led to impaired reactivation of Pol II genes as cells enter G1 phase.
source: Previously, we have shown that depletion of TBP in mESCs specifically during mitosis led to impaired reactivation of Pol II genes as cells enter G1 phase (Teves et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The heat shock response leads to rapid transcriptional induction of heat shock protein genes.
source: A highly conserved protective mechanism to various stressors, the HS response leads to rapid transcriptional induction of HS protein genes (DiDomenico et al., 1982).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Gene browser tracks and heatmaps for CUT&Tag and NET-seq at HS genes show massive increases in occupancy and activity upon HS compared to control samples.
source: Gene browser tracks and heatmaps for CUT&Tag and NET-seq at HS genes show massive increases in occupancy and activity upon HS compared to control samples (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by CUT&Tag and NET-seq data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: 392 and 374 genes are significantly upregulated and downregulated, respectively, in HS samples compared to control.
source: DGE analysis of Pol II CUT&Tag data shows that 392 and 374 genes are significantly upregulated and downregulated, respectively, in HS samples compared to control (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 3C and listed in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of the upregulated genes showed markers that are typically enriched for HS response.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the upregulated genes showed markers that are typically enriched for HS response, further confirming proper HS induction (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis listed in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Under HS + IAA conditions, gene browser tracks for Pol II CUT&Tag and NET-seq at HS genes show that these genes are still induced upon TBP depletion.
source: Under HS + IAA conditions, gene browser tracks for Pol II CUT&Tag and NET-seq at HS genes show that these genes are still induced upon TBP depletion (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by gene browser tracks shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DGE analysis of Pol II CUT&Tag for HS versus HS + IAA samples shows no significant changes in gene expression.
source: DGE analysis of Pol II CUT&Tag for HS versus HS + IAA samples shows no significant changes in gene expression (Figure 3D), indicating that global expression changes induced by HS still occur upon TBP depletion.
evidence: Supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Global expression changes induced by HS still occur upon TBP depletion.
source: DGE analysis of Pol II CUT&Tag for HS versus HS + IAA samples shows no significant changes in gene expression (Figure 3D), indicating that global expression changes induced by HS still occur upon TBP depletion.
evidence: Inferred from the DGE analysis showing no significant changes between HS and HS + IAA conditions.

claim: Depletion of TBP does not impair Pol II induction of HS genes.
source: These results suggest that depletion of TBP does not impair Pol II induction of HS genes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HS genes are still induced upon TBP depletion.

claim: The HS response is a classical gene induction system regulated at the level of paused Pol II elongation.
source: The HS response is a classical gene induction system regulated at the level of paused Pol II elongation (Core and Adelman, 2019), and HS genes may retain a scaffold of PIC components following promoter pausing release.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HS genes may retain a scaffold of PIC components following promoter pausing release.
source: The HS response is a classical gene induction system regulated at the level of paused Pol II elongation (Core and Adelman, 2019), and HS genes may retain a scaffold of PIC components following promoter pausing release.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors to explain why HS genes may not require TBP for induction.

claim: RA-mediated differentiation of C64 mESCs leads to the silencing of pluripotency markers and activation of ectoderm-specific genes.
source: Therefore, we also examined the role of TBP in an orthogonal gene activation system through RA-mediated differentiation of C64 mESCs, which leads to the silencing of pluripotency markers and activation of ectoderm-specific genes (Semrau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Gene browser tracks of Stra8 and Cdx1 genes show significant increases in Pol II occupancy after RA treatment.
source: Gene browser tracks of Stra8 and Cdx1 genes show significant increases in Pol II occupancy after RA treatment (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by gene browser tracks shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The pluripotency marker Myc displays a large decrease in Pol II occupancy under RA conditions.
source: Additionally, the pluripotency marker Myc displays a large decrease in Pol II occupancy under RA conditions (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by gene browser tracks shown in Figure 3F.

claim: DGE analysis of Pol II CUT&Tag revealed 44 upregulated and 88 downregulated genes after RA treatment.
source: DGE analysis of Pol II CUT&Tag revealed 44 upregulated and 88 downregulated genes, confirming proper RA induction (Figure 3G, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 3G and listed in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Gene browser tracks for Pol II CUT&Tag at the Stra8 gene show similar levels of Pol II binding in both RA and RA + IAA conditions.
source: Gene browser tracks for Pol II CUT&Tag at the Stra8 gene, a RA-mediated gene, show similar levels of Pol II binding in both RA and RA + IAA conditions (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by gene browser tracks shown in Figure 3F.

claim: DGE analysis of Pol II CUT&Tag data for RA and RA + IAA samples showed no significant differences between the two conditions.
source: DGE analysis of Pol II CUT&Tag data for RA and RA + IAA samples (Figure 3H) also showed no significant differences between the two conditions.
evidence: Supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Depleting TBP does not affect the activation of RA-specific genes.
source: Finally, we plotted the Pol II occupancy for the 44 significantly upregulated genes extracted from DGE analysis for RA and RA + IAA treatment as heatmaps centered at the TSS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F). Both RA and RA + IAA conditions display similar levels of Pol II, confirming that depleting TBP does not affect the activation of RA-specific genes.
evidence: Supported by heatmap data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: TBP is dispensable for both ongoing transcription and gene induction.
